hints: Focus on what first ionisation energy actually describes, removing one electron from a neutral gaseous atom.
Remember the starting point must be one mole of separate $\text{Br(g)}$ atoms, not $\text{Br}_2\text{(g)}$ molecules.
Look for the equation that forms one mole of $\text{Br}^+\text{(g)}$ plus one electron, with no extra bond breaking or electron gain involved.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of first ionisation energy**

First ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-$$

**Apply it to bromine**

For bromine, X is $\text{Br}$, so we need $\text{Br(g)}$ on the left and $\text{Br}^+\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-$ on the right.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Br(g)} \rightarrow \text{Br}^+\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-$$

**Check state symbols and starting species**

All species must be gaseous, and we must start from atomic bromine. Starting from $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{Br}_2\text{(g)}$ would include the energy to break the Br-Br bond, so it is not pure ionisation.

options.A: This matches the definition exactly. One mole of gaseous Br atoms loses one electron each to form $\text{Br}^+\text{(g)}$. No bond breaking or other change is included.
options.B: This forms $\text{Br}^-\text{(g)}$, which is electron gain not electron loss. It is related to electron affinity, not ionisation energy. Writing $- \text{e}^-$ is also incorrect for ionisation.
options.C: Although the products are correct, the reactant is $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{Br}_2\text{(g)}$. This energy change includes half the Br-Br bond dissociation energy plus the ionisation energy, so it is too large.
options.D: This is wrong twice. It starts from $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{Br}_2\text{(g)}$ so includes bond breaking, and it forms $\text{Br}^-\text{(g)}$ which is electron affinity chemistry, not ionisation.
